title: 2014: Microsoft opens the code
cards/0/body:
In the early 2000s Microsoft called open source a threat. In 2014, under new CEO Satya Nadella, it open-sourced .NET.

The reason was practical: servers increasingly ran Linux, and a Windows-only platform was losing to Java, Node.js and Go.
cards/1/body:
Roslyn: the C# and VB compiler, written in C# itself. Analyzers and IDE hints use its API.

.NET Foundation: an independent foundation for open-source projects.

.NET Core: a new cross-platform .NET under the MIT license, developed in the open on GitHub.
cards/3/options/0: The C# and VB compiler with an open API, written in C#
cards/3/explain: Analyzers, refactorings and source generators all run on Roslyn.
cards/4/q: What does the MIT license allow?
cards/4/options/0: You can use, change and sell the code as long as you keep the copyright notice
cards/4/options/1: You can only read the code
cards/4/options/2: You can use it only in non-commercial projects
cards/4/explain: It is one of the most permissive licenses around.
cards/5/q: Why did Microsoft open up .NET? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: Servers and clouds ran Linux at scale
cards/5/options/1: Competitors (Java, Node.js, Go) were open and cross-platform
cards/5/options/2: The community can send in fixes
cards/5/options/3: It ran out of money for development
cards/5/explain: Today a noticeable share of changes in dotnet/runtime comes from people outside Microsoft.
cards/6/q: Match each name to what it is
cards/7/q: Where can you read the source of List<T> or the garbage collector today?
cards/7/options/0: In the open dotnet repos on GitHub
cards/7/explain: You can even step through it in a debugger: Source Link fetches the sources for you.
